content: Each year, approximately 450,000 children globally succumb to pneumococcal infections. The increasing resistance of bacteria to antimicrobial treatments complicates disease management and underscores the importance of preventive strategies. While newborn vaccination schedules significantly reduce pneumococcal disease in immunized children, they do not address the morbidity and mortality of infants under three months of age. Administering pneumococcal vaccines during pregnancy has been proposed as a potential method to protect infants during their first months of life, prior to the onset of protection from direct infant vaccination. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccination during pregnancy in preventing infections in infants. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of July 31, 2014) and reference lists of relevant studies. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing pneumococcal vaccination in pregnant women with placebo, no intervention, or other vaccines. Seven trials were identified, but only six trials involving 919 participants provided usable data. The evidence did not demonstrate that pneumococcal vaccination during pregnancy reduces the risk of neonatal infection (risk ratio [RR] 0.66; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.30 to 1.46; two trials, 241 pregnancies; low-quality evidence). Although one trial suggested a reduction in pneumococcal colonization in infants by 16 months of age (average RR 0.33; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.98; 56 pregnancies), no such effect was observed in infants at two to three months (average RR 1.13; 95% CI 0.46 to 2.78; two trials, 146 pregnancies; low-quality evidence) or at six to seven months (average RR 0.67; 95% CI 0.22 to 2.08; two trials, 148 pregnancies; low-quality evidence). None of the trials reported neonatal deaths due to pneumococcal infection. Neonatal antibody levels were reported as geometric means with 95% CIs, but the results were inconsistent across studies. Two studies found significantly higher immunoglobulin G (IgG) levels in cord blood in the pneumococcal vaccine group compared to controls for all serotypes. However, another trial found no difference in neonatal antibody levels between the vaccinated and control groups. Maternal antibody levels were also reported as geometric means with 95% CIs. One study observed significantly higher IgG levels in maternal serum in the pneumococcal vaccine group across all serotypes, while another study found higher maternal antibody levels only for serotype 14, with no effect for other serotypes. One trial measured the percentage of women with seroprotection at delivery and 12 months postpartum. At delivery, the intervention group showed higher seroprotection for serotype 6 (RR 1.49; 95% CI 1.31 to 1.69), serotype 14 (RR 1.40; 95% CI 1.25 to 1.56), and serotype 19 (RR 2.29; 95% CI 1.89 to 2.76). At 12 months postpartum, no differences were observed for serotypes 6 or 14 (RR 1.06; 95% CI 1.00 to 1.12 and RR 1.06; 95% CI 0.98 to 1.15, respectively), but serotype 19 still favored the intervention group (RR 1.59; 95% CI 1.37 to 1.85). Regarding safety, there was no significant difference in tenderness at the injection site between women who received the pneumococcal vaccine and those who received a control vaccine (average RR 3.20; 95% CI 0.32 to 31.54; two trials, 130 women). The overall quality of evidence for the primary outcomes was low. Most outcomes had wide confidence intervals that crossed the line of no effect, and the small sample sizes and low event rates in the included trials contributed to the imprecision of the findings. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether pneumococcal vaccination during pregnancy effectively reduces infant infections.
